newsitem.title: POLAND: Low demand seen boosting Polish T-bill yields.
newsitem.headline: Low demand seen boosting Polish T-bill yields.

text.p: Polish T-bill yields are likely to extend last week's jump at Monday's 1.2 billion primary tender on low demand as players are likely to wait for prices to hit bottom before returning to the market, dealers said.

"Primary T-bill yields are likely to rise again on Monday and we may see the 52-week T-bill maximum yield at 21 percent," said Piotr Bednarek from ING Bank in Warsaw. The yield was last at 20.83 percent.

Dealers expected demand would not even cover half of the offer, though it might inch up to around 500 million zlotys from last auction's 362 million, as many banks still expected yields would top 21 percent.
"A substantial rise in demand will signal that T-bill yields are approaching their ceiling, but this will not happen this Monday," ING's Bednarek said.
Half year paper was expected to yield a maximum of 20.70-80 percent and 13-week T-bills some 20.60-70 percent from the last auction's 20.64 and 20.47 percent respectively.
Dealers said the longest 52-week T-bill yield should reach its ceiling at 21.40-50 percent. They said such yield level could draw foreign capital and give the zloty a boost.
"If the Polish 52-week bill goes above 21 percent it may trigger a wave of foreign investment," said Wojciech Kowalczyk from Bank Handlowy SA.
Traders began bidding for higher yields after the finance ministry said earlier this month it would accept a yield rise because it badly needed cash to finance the budget gap.
It also boosted its T-bill offer in March to 4.9 billion zlotys from four billion in February, signalling higher borrowing needs.
But the ministry has said it would not let T-bill yields rise to match yields of NBP-bills, last around 22 percent, because it would cost the budget too much.
The March offer includes two 8-week bill offers of 400 million zlotys each which analysts said were aimed at the corporate sector, usually keen on shorter investment.
"The treasury offered 8-week T-bills to attract corporate money," said Krzysztof Syska from PKO BP.

Dealers expected large foreign entry at Wednesday's 800 million zloty 15-percent two-year and 12-percent five-year bond tender. "The demand and yield structure at the fixed bond tender should be the same as last time," said ING's Bednarek.
Foreigners bought the majority of the 550 million zlotys of Polish 12-percent five-year bonds sold on February 5.

The zloty was seen consolidating within its present range against the basket of currencies next week after it was capped by central bank interventions at three percent from the parity rate earlier in February.
"The zloty should stay between 2.8 and three percent from parity next week," said a dealer at a major Polish bank.
It closed the week at 3.02/2.99 percent from the parity rate, slightly higher than last Friday's 2.98/2.90 percent.
One-day deposits were seen trading at above 22 percent next week after the NBP raised obligatory reserve requirements for both zloty and currency deposits.
"One-day rates are likely to trade above 22 percent next week because of the higher reserve requirements," said Malgorzata Sikora from ING Bank in Warsaw.
Overnight deposits closed the week at 22.00/22.20 percent, and tomorrow/next rates at 22.00/22.55 percent.
